strengths: FaceXFormer addresses a practical computer vision problem: consolidating dense, geometric, semantic, and identity-related facial analysis into one framework. Supporting ten tasks could simplify deployment and large-scale annotation.

The evaluation covers numerous established benchmarks and reports competitive results, including 3.52 MAE on BIWI, 3.05 full-set NME on 300W, and 91.83% attribute accuracy on CelebA. A unified model need not outperform every specialist to be useful.

Table 7 provides evidence that bidirectional attention helps within the proposed architecture: head-pose MAE improves from 4.63 to 3.52 and age MAE from 4.84 to 4.17. Appendix D also provides encouraging cross-dataset landmark results.

The reported efficiency is promising: 33.2 versus 14.3 FPS and 109.29 versus 178.9 million parameters compared with Faceptor. The manuscript provides optimization and augmentation details, cites its datasets and losses, and explicitly considers licensing and demographic disparities.
weaknesses: The central architectural novelty is insufficiently established. FaceX's token self-attention, token-to-image attention, image-to-token attention, two-layer structure, and segmentation readout closely resemble SAM's two-way decoder. SAM [40] is cited as background, but this architectural relationship is neither attributed precisely nor differentiated. The paper needs to distinguish its contribution as a facial multitask adaptation from its claim of a novel attention mechanism.

Table 3 contains a material numerical inconsistency: FaceXFormer's ten class F1 scores average to 91.01, not 92.01. All listed baseline means agree with their class scores. The corrected value retains a small lead over Faceptor's 90.89, but reduces the claimed improvement from 1.12 to 0.12 points. This is correctable, yet substantially changes the headline parsing result.

Simultaneous performance from one model is insufficiently documented. Section 4.2 mentions three additional training epochs for unspecified tasks without clarifying whether every reported result uses the same final checkpoint. Appendix F retains different alignment/cropping procedures for recognition, landmarks, and pose, without quantitative evaluation using a common input pipeline. Furthermore, no quantitative race-prediction result is provided despite race being one of the ten claimed tasks.

Important reproducibility details remain unresolved: loss weights, exact age-evaluation splits, and mappings between incompatible age/race label schemes are unspecified. Appendix F.5 introduces MORPH-II training and evaluation, whereas the main dataset list omits MORPH-II and Table 4 labels the age results as UTKFace. These discrepancies affect interpretation and comparability of the results.

The experiments do not isolate the benefits of task sharing. There is no matched-backbone, matched-data comparison against separately trained tasks or a simpler shared-backbone model with independent heads. Table 7 tests attention components, but does not establish the claimed positive task transfer or show that bidirectional attention uniquely enables an effective shallow decoder.

The runtime comparison lacks an explicit inference hardware, batch-size, preprocessing, and resolution protocol. Different backbone and resolution choices are not controlled, and decoder depth is not systematically varied. Consequently, the reported speed advantage does not establish the claim that the proposed decoder is its principal cause.

The conclusion of minimal demographic bias overstates Table 8. Aggregating six racial categories into 'Non-white' can conceal subgroup disparities, and the age accuracy gap of 0.50 exceeds CLIP's absolute gap of 0.30 and FaRL's 0.35. No ablation supports the causal attribution of reduced bias to race co-training.
